concept.body: Field method, every time: sketch the right triangle; mark the horizontal; place the angle; write each length's role FROM that angle (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse); choose the ratio containing your known and unknown; multiply if the unknown is on top, divide if it's on the bottom; then sanity-check against the longest-side rule.

explanationVariants: tan 45° = h/25 with tan 45° = 1, so h = 25 m — a 45° sun makes shadow equal height.
At 45° the legs match: height = shadow = 25 m.

widget.prompt: The sun is at exactly 45°. A flagpole casts a 25 m shadow. The pole's height = ? (m)

commonErrors.feedback: 17.68 ≈ 25·sin 45° treats the shadow as a hypotenuse — it's the ground LEG. tan 45° = 1 makes h = 25.
35.36 ≈ 25 ÷ cos 45° computes the sun-ray slant. The height equals the shadow at 45°: 25 m.

steps.body: Shadows are free measuring tape. The sun's elevation angle plus a shadow's length pins an object's height — the same similar-triangles idea from the Similarity course, now with trig doing the ratio work. Height opposite, shadow adjacent: **tan(sun angle) = height/shadow**, whichever piece is missing.

explanationVariants: The shadow is adjacent, on the bottom of the tangent: 12 ÷ tan 38° ≈ 15.36 m.

widget.prompt: The sun is at 38° elevation. How long a shadow does a 12 m tree cast, in meters (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 9.38 = 12·tan 38° multiplies — but the shadow s is on the BOTTOM of tan 38° = 12/s. Divide: ≈ 15.36.
19.49 = 12 ÷ sin 38° computes the sun-ray's slant length (hypotenuse), not the ground shadow: ≈ 15.36.
7.39 = 12·sin 38° treats the 12 m tree as a hypotenuse — it's the vertical LEG. s = 12 ÷ tan 38° ≈ 15.36.

steps.body: Cables and guy wires flip the unknown to the **hypotenuse**. A pole of height 18 m needs a wire meeting the ground at 65°: the pole is opposite, the wire is the hypotenuse — sin 65° = 18/w, so w = 18 ÷ sin 65° ≈ 19.86 m. Unknown on the bottom: divide.

explanationVariants: sin 65° = 18/w → w = 18 ÷ sin 65° ≈ 19.86 m — barely longer than the pole, since 65° is steep.
Opposite known, hypotenuse wanted: divide by the sine. 18 ÷ 0.9063 ≈ 19.86 m.

widget.prompt: A guy wire runs from the top of an 18 m pole to the ground, meeting it at 65°. How long is the wire (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 16.31 = 18·sin 65° multiplies — giving a wire SHORTER than the pole it must reach over. Divide: 18 ÷ sin 65° ≈ 19.86.
42.59 = 18 ÷ cos 65° pairs the pole with cosine — but the pole is OPPOSITE the 65° ground angle, sine's side: ≈ 19.86.
38.6 = 18·tan 65° relates the two LEGS — the wire is the hypotenuse, which tangent never gives. ≈ 19.86.

widget.prompt: Every applied trig problem starts the same way. What comes FIRST?

options.label: Draw the triangle and label each side's role from the given angle
options.feedback: The picture decides everything after it — sides labeled from the angle make the ratio choice automatic.

options.label: Punch the angle into the calculator
options.feedback: A calculator can't tell sine from tangent for you — the picture assigns the roles. Sketch first, compute last.

options.label: Guess whether to multiply or divide
options.feedback: Multiply-vs-divide is READ off the setup (unknown on top or bottom), never guessed. The sketch comes first.

options.label: Convert the angle to radians
options.feedback: Degrees are fine throughout this course — and units never assign side roles. Draw and label first.

steps.body: The professional trick: **two readings**. From point A the tower top sits at 40° elevation; walk 30 m closer to B and it reads 55°. Two triangles share the same height h: h = x·tan 55° (near) and h = (x + 30)·tan 40° (far). Two equations, two unknowns — no need to reach the tower at all.

explanationVariants: Same h both ways: x·tan 55° = (x + 30)·tan 40° — solve for x, then h = x·tan 55°.
Setting the near expression equal to the far one eliminates h and leaves one unknown, x.

widget.prompt: In the two-reading setup, which equation lets you find x (the near distance)?

options.label: x·tan 55° = (x + 30)·tan 40°
options.feedback: Both sides equal the tower's height h — equating them removes h and solves for x.

options.label: x·tan 40° = (x + 30)·tan 55°
options.feedback: The angles are swapped: the NEAR point sees the steeper 55°, the far point the shallower 40°. As written, x would come out negative.

options.label: x + 30 = tan 55° − tan 40°
options.feedback: That equates a distance to a difference of RATIOS — mismatched quantities. Set the two height expressions equal instead.

options.label: h = 30·tan 55° + 30·tan 40°
options.feedback: Adding the two readings' heights double-counts — the 30 m isn't the distance to the tower from either point. Equate x·tan 55° with (x + 30)·tan 40°.

widget.prompt: In that setup, x·tan 55° = (x + 30)·tan 40° gives x ≈ 42.74 m. Roughly what is the FAR point's distance to the tower, in meters (2 decimals)?

commonErrors.feedback: 42.74 is x itself — the NEAR distance. The far point stands 30 m further back: 42.74 + 30 = 72.74.
12.74 subtracts the 30 m — but B moved CLOSER, so A is x + 30 from the tower: 72.74.

hints: h = x·tan 55° with x ≈ 42.74 — or equivalently h = 72.74·tan 40°.
explanationVariants: h = x·tan 55° ≈ 42.74 × 1.4281 ≈ 61.03 m — and the far check, 72.74·tan 40°, lands on the same value.
Either triangle works once x is known: h ≈ 61.03 m.

widget.prompt: Finish the survey: with x ≈ 42.74 m, find the tower's height h in meters (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 25.17 = 30·tan 40° uses the 30 m WALK as if it were the distance to the tower — it's only the gap between readings. h = x·tan 55° ≈ 61.03.
42.84 = 30·tan 55° makes the same substitution with the other angle. Use the near distance: 42.74·tan 55° ≈ 61.03.
35.86 = 42.74·tan 40° pairs the NEAR distance with the FAR angle — mixed triangles. Matching pairs: 42.74·tan 55° ≈ 61.03.

takeaways: Shadows: tan(sun angle) = height/shadow — solve for either piece.
Wires and cables are hypotenuses: divide by sine (or cosine) to size them.
Two readings from different spots pin an unreachable height: equate the two h-expressions.
steps.teaser: Last chapter: how sin, cos, and tan relate to each other — and what survives when the right angle leaves.
